title: Ranveer Singh Just Took India's Biggest Film to Japan. The Numbers Are Obscene.
excerpt: Dhurandhar opens in Tokyo today with a ₹3,100 crore franchise behind it — and Saif Ali Khan just declared there's a 'before and after Dhurandhar' era in Bollywood.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dhurandhar franchise grossed ₹3,100 crore worldwide, redefining Hindi cinema's commercial landscape.
  • The sequel, Dhurandhar: The Revenge, is the 3rd highest-grossing Indian film ever.
  • Ranveer Singh's special message targets Japanese audiences, marking a strategic release.
  • Saif Ali Khan claims Dhurandhar marks a pivotal shift in Bollywood's approach to filmmaking.
  • Dhurandhar's success is reshaping global perceptions of Indian cinema.

Article data
https://youtube.com/watch?v=EOIa-mRaQ7M There is a moment, in the life of a franchise, when it stops being a film and becomes a weather system. **Dhurandhar** hit that moment sometime around its second weekend, when it became clear that Aditya Dhar hadn't just made a spy thriller — he'd rewired the entire commercial grammar of Hindi cinema. Today, as the first installment opens in theatres across Japan, the franchise's combined worldwide gross sits at a casually staggering **₹3,100 crore**. Let that number breathe for a second. ![Saif Ali Khan — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8b/Saif_SG_screening.jpg) > **"*Dhurandhar: The Revenge* recently dropped on **Netflix in the US and Canada** in a special "raw and uncut" version that didn't play in Indian theatres."** The Japan release is strategic, not sentimental. **Ranveer Singh** recorded a special video message for Japanese audiences — a personal invitation to experience the scale and intensity of the film on the big screen. It's the kind of move Hollywood studios make routinely but Indian productions almost never bother with. The Japanese market has recently shown genuine enthusiasm for large-scale Indian blockbusters, and Jio Studios is betting that Dhurandhar's grounded-yet-massive action spectacle will translate. The franchise arithmetic is worth laying out. The first installment — in which Ranveer plays Hamza Ali Mazari, an undercover agent caught in a high-stakes geopolitical web — currently holds the **5th spot on the all-time Indian box office chart** with a lifetime worldwide collection of **₹1,307 crore**. Its sequel, *Dhurandhar: The Revenge*, is the real monster: a worldwide gross north of **₹1,813 crore**, making it the **3rd highest-grossing Indian film of all time** and the **first purely Hindi-language film to cross ₹1,000 crore net in India**. The sequel is now on the verge of overtaking *Baahubali 2: The Conclusion* for the number two spot globally. For NRI audiences, there's a separate timeline running in parallel. *Dhurandhar: The Revenge* recently dropped on **Netflix in the US and Canada** in a special "raw and uncut" version that didn't play in Indian theatres. The international streaming premiere arrived about eight weeks after the theatrical run, and includes footage that the Indian theatrical cut trimmed. If you're in North America and haven't caught the sequel yet, it's streaming now — with extra heat. But the Japan release is about something bigger than territory expansion. It's about what Dhurandhar has done to the conversation around Hindi cinema itself. ![Aditya Dhar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Aditya_Dhar_at_IFFI_2019_%28cropped%29.jpg) **Saif Ali Khan** put it bluntly in a new interview with *The Hollywood Reporter India* that went viral this week. "I see a time before Dhurandhar and a time after," he said. "It's up to us whether we catch up or not and wake up or not." Coming from an actor who's been in the industry for three decades, that's not a casual observation — it's a diagnosis. Khan praised the franchise's revolutionary approach to music, arguing that Shashwat Sachdev's score — blending original compositions like *Shararat* and *Gehra Hu* with bold remixes — showed that Indian filmmakers should draw from global influences without fear. The cultural footprint extends beyond the screen. Just this week, Ranveer surfaced at **Anshula Kapoor and Rohan Thakkar's wedding reception** in Mumbai, arriving with heavy security and minimal paparazzi interaction — a post-Dhurandhar reality for the actor, who has reportedly received threats. But once inside, the man who embodies Bollywood's most electric energy was back. The DJ played Dhurandhar tracks, the crowd erupted, and Ranveer reunited with **Arjun Kapoor** to recreate their legendary *'Tune Maari Entriyaan'* from *Gunday*. Videos from the reception flooded social media within hours.
Cultural Impact of Dhurandhar
›Saif Ali Khan sees a 'before and after' Dhurandhar era.
›Franchise blends global influences in music and storytelling.
›Ranveer Singh's presence at events reflects heightened celebrity status.
›Dhurandhar's success is a point of pride for the Indian diaspora.
> "I see a time before Dhurandhar and a time after. It's up to us whether we catch up or not and wake up or not." — Saif Ali Khan Meanwhile, the man behind the camera isn't resting. Director **Aditya Dhar** has built something that the Hindi film industry hasn't seen before: a franchise where both installments independently sit in the all-time top five. The ensemble — Sanjay Dutt, Akshaye Khanna, R. Madhavan, Arjun Rampal, Sara Arjun — has the depth of a prestige ensemble cast with the commercial instincts of a blockbuster machine. And Ranveer? His next move is equally audacious. **Pralay**, a ₹300 crore post-apocalyptic zombie thriller directed by Jai Mehta (of *Scam 1992* fame), is locked for a September shoot in Australia. Filming will merge physical sets with AI-driven visuals, and South Indian star **Kalyani Priyadarshan** — fresh off her blockbuster *Lokah* — makes her Hindi debut opposite him. For the diaspora watching from abroad, the Dhurandhar phenomenon is a point of pride that keeps growing. A Hindi-language spy thriller conquering Japan, streaming uncensored on Netflix globally, and fundamentally altering how Bollywood thinks about scale, music, and ambition — this isn't just a franchise. It's a before-and-after moment. Saif said it best.
